Niché en plein cœur de la Petite-Italie,: Nestled in the heart of Little Italy, the restaurant Nouveau Système has been a fixture on its street since 1962.

À peine entré dans le restaurant, on se: You’ve barely stepped inside the restaurant and you feel transported straight back to the 1960s. Through the glass door and front window, you can see a long room striped in red and white, a sign of a not-so-distant time when that combination of colours told passersby they could surely find a quick bite to eat.
À droite, le long du mur, des tables en: On the right, along the wall, Formica tables framed by American-style booths sit beneath a jukebox. On its playlists: Tina Turner, Carlos Santana, Eric Clapton and several other icons of an era that has almost passed. Opposite, the long counter and its metal stools overlook the kitchen, where cooks, busboys and waitresses bustle like an anthill.
À hauteur de regard, des enseignes Coca-: At eye level, Coca-Cola signs and pop art–style prints display prices from another era: best poutine in town for 25 cents, hamburger for 5 cents. And, the centrepiece of this vintage world, a large round mirror showcases the house specialty for more than 50 years now: the Nouveau Système hot dog.
Carmen connaît bien le restaurant situé: Carmen knows the restaurant at 363 Beaubien Street well. The 65-year-old retiree comes every day. As usual, she takes a seat at the counter, orders her usual coffee and strikes up a conversation with the staff.
« Je suis née pas loin d’ici, sur la rue: “I was born not far from here, on Casgrain Street. I grew up in the neighbourhood. I live five minutes from here, so I’m here all the time. I really like the atmosphere, and everyone is nice. Here, it’s a bit like my second home,” she says between sips.
“My mother came here for 30 years. My uncle still comes here, and from time to time we come together. And I remember having my first dates here, when I was 17 or 18. We’d sit right there,” she says, pointing to the table at the back of the restaurant.
Derrière son comptoir et son tablier bla: Behind his counter, in his white cook’s apron, George Giannaras seems absorbed by the big pot of tomato sauce he is preparing. It’s Sunday afternoon, and the relative calm is ideal for the little jobs you never have time for when it’s too busy. His movements are sure and fluid, but his words are few. The restaurateur is in action, like the rest of his team.
George Ganiarras est le propriétaire à l: George Ganiarras has been the owner at the helm of the snack bar for almost 37 years. He was barely 20 when he went into business. Photo: Katharine Norva
George, le propriétaire du Nouveau Systè: George, the owner of Nouveau Système, was born in the Rosemont neighbourhood to parents who had arrived from Greece in the early 1960s. The family was then living on Masson Street above the restaurant run by his father, John, who would later take over several similar establishments.
Il n’est donc pas surprenant que George,: So it’s no surprise that George, who grew up in this world of stoves and kitchen smells, decided one day to have his own restaurant.
C’est d’ailleurs grâce à son père qu’il: It was also thanks to his father that he raised the funds needed to buy Nouveau Système. “After high school, I started working at my cousin’s restaurant. All the money I earned, I put aside in the bank. I only took my tips. And at one point I went to see my father and told him: I have $20,000, I want to invest it in a restaurant. He said okay. He put in another $20,000, and we became owners on March 1<sup>st</sup>, 1987; I was 20,” he says, without ever lifting his eyes from the pizza dough taking shape.
Depuis près de 37 ans, donc, George s’oc: So for almost 37 years, George has looked after his pizzas, his hot dogs and his customers. “I don’t like change, I prefer stability and work done right. A lot of people say, ‘It’s just a cheeseburger.’ But no, your meat has to be properly cooked, even if [the pace of work] is fast and you have to send out several at once. That’s why a lot of other restaurants close. Me, I love what I do and I’m meticulous.”
C’est cet esprit qui imprègne le goût de: That spirit permeates the taste of every dish the restaurant serves, faithful to its recipes and its tradition. Same coleslaw hot dogs, same poutine, everything here seems frozen in time. “The poutine sauce is the same one we’ve always used; it’s the recipe invented by George’s father!” says Jean-Pierre, the place’s jack-of-all-trades, who has just joined the conversation.
Toujours prêt à entamer une conversation: Always ready to start a conversation between rounds of dishes, Jean-Pierre, who gladly broke away from a boring retirement, has worked here for almost five years. “I used to come here as a customer. I’d see my friend Danielle, one of the waitresses, and everyone else swamped. I told myself that giving some of my time couldn’t hurt. I came here out of friendship first.”
C’est encore par amitié qu’au fil des an: It’s also out of friendship that, over the years, Jean-Pierre has bonded with all his regulars, including André and Jean-Claude, who don’t hesitate to confide their secrets to him and share their worries and joys. For the most part, the regulars have salt-and-pepper hair and enjoy the company of the young people and families who come by on occasion, in the evening and on weekends, at Nouveau Système.
Jean-Pierre – comme tous les autres empl: Jean-Pierre – like all the other employees of the restaurant – knows what each of them will order. But he also knows about their aches and pains, and never hesitates to offer advice or crack a joke to comfort them.
Ici, on s’inquiète pour untel, qui a per: Here, people worry about so-and-so, who has lost a loved one; about another, who was arrested by the police; or about a regular looking for housing. What is said around the counter at Nouveau Système goes well beyond the menu. Here, they’re family, they sympathize, they try to help each other. In these times of chronic indifference, that’s no small thing.

Quiconque met les pieds régulièrement au: Anyone who regularly sets foot in Nouveau Système knows Jimmy. George’s cousin and right-hand man is a cook. Cap screwed on his head, a mischievous look in his eye, Jimmy is always ready to bring a smile to the faces of colleagues and customers. “I’m the best chef in the world, better than Gordon Ramsay!” he jokes.
C’est à l’âge de 14 ans que le Gordon Ra: It was at the age of 14 that the Gordon Ramsay of Beaubien Street dove into the trade. He learned the ropes in his father’s restaurant, then much later bought his first restaurant with his brother. The venture lasted about fifteen years, until they sold it. “When my brother decided to go live in Greece, I told myself: ‘No, it’s hard enough running a restaurant, I don’t want to do it alone.’” But since a person has to make a living, Jimmy put his apron back on as an employee in the kitchen at Nouveau Système. It was 2008, and the face of Little Italy was changing more and more.
« Avant, il y avait des jeunes <em>kids: “Before, there were young kids who came here after school. There were lots of immigrant families living around here, you could see Latinos, Italians, Haitians. I remember, sometimes the kids would invite me to go play soccer at Parc de Gaspé next door. It was fun,” says Jimmy.
Peu à peu, ces familles ont dû quitter l: Little by little, those families had to leave the neighbourhood because of rents that kept climbing. “Now, the ones who replaced them are rich kids, with parents who are civil servants or lawyers who can afford to pay. They’re yuppies. It has nothing to do with the people you used to see walking around the neighbourhood.”
De cela, Angelo peut également témoigner: Angelo can vouch for that too. Leaning on the counter to chat with the owner, the businessman, who works in real estate, has been coming to Nouveau Système since the early 1980s. Back then, he owned the music store next door. He only had to take three steps to come enjoy George’s pizza, and George eventually became a friend. “George puts love in his pizza. Anywhere else, you won’t get that. Why would I go elsewhere? I know the people here. I feel at home here.”
Né en Italie, Angelo est arrivé à Montré: Born in Italy, Angelo arrived in Montréal at the age of 10. His family settled in the neighbourhood, whose streets and façades he knows by heart. By the end of the 1970s, fewer and fewer Italian immigrants were settling in the parish. Then, like other members of his community, Angelo left Little Italy as soon as the chance to own a home came up. “There were a lot of Italians here. You still see Italian businesses along Saint-Laurent and on Dante Street, but the Italians themselves are gone. People climb the ladder and want to become homeowners. So they went farther north: Saint-Michel, Montréal-Nord, Saint-Léonard, Chomedey,” says the man who now lives in Laval.
L’homme n’en reste pas moins attaché à l: He remains attached to Little Italy nonetheless, and goes there regularly. “The church at the corner of Saint-Zotique and Saint-Laurent, actually, it was turned into condos. It was sold because nobody was going anymore. Rich people live there,” says Angelo, who regrets that the neighbourhood has lost some of its authenticity.
Il y a aussi la vitalité économique de l: Little Italy’s economic vitality is also in question. George, who has watched things unfold for 37 years, has some worries. “Every four or five years, one business closes and another moves in, only to close later in its turn. It’s always the same thing.” Times are indeed tough for business. With inflation hitting hard, the aftershocks of the pandemic and the exorbitant cost of commercial leases due to gentrification, staying afloat as a merchant is a tightrope act.
Mais il en faut plus pour effrayer John,: But it takes more than that to scare John, George’s eldest son, who wants to take over the restaurant and continue the family adventure.
Tout juste âgé de 20 ans, John alterne e: Just 20 years old, John divides his time between studies in accounting and his hours at Nouveau Système.
John est le fils du propriétaire. Il asp: John is the owner’s son. He aspires to carry on the work of his father George and to usher Nouveau Système into a new era. Photo: Khady Konaté
« J’ai commencé à venir ici régulièremen: “I started coming here regularly and working here three years ago. At first, I didn’t really feel like I belonged, but I got used to it. You know, our parents and grandparents fought to make a living, so that their children could succeed. So working, and working here, is a way of honouring their sacrifices,” he explains
Sur l’écran qui domine la salle, on diff: On the screen above the room, the latest adaptation of King Kong is playing. Just like at home, people here watch whatever’s on – a hockey game, a news bulletin, everything is material for discussion.
Aux côtés de son père, John comprend ce: Alongside his father, John understands what having a work ethic means. He has also drawn other lessons from working at the restaurant: “This place has taught me an enormous amount. I learn more about society when I come here, every time a new person walks into the restaurant, whether they’re rich or poor, it doesn’t matter. Here we talk, we eat and we laugh.”
Le jeune homme croit au potentiel de l’e: The young man believes in the place’s potential to remain a neighbourhood staple, but also wants to develop it and usher it into a new era. He hopes to do so by recruiting young people of his generation to freshen up the business while preserving its authentic character. “I want to take the restaurant to a new level because we’ve been stagnating for a while. I want to make it evolve.”
Seule certitude, le Nouveau Système, ave: One thing is certain: Nouveau Système, with its hot dogs, fries, hamburgers and vintage look, will always be that meeting place where it feels good to find one another.
